TURKISH ADAPTATION OF THE SELF-COMPASSION SCALE SHORT FORM: VALIDITY AND RELIABILITY STUDY*
Musa YILDIRIM**
Tuğba SARI*** ABSTRACT The aim of this study was to examine the psychometric properties of the Turkish version of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form among adolescents. For this purpose, data were collected from 800 adolescents—400 middle school students and 400 high school students. In order to examine the psychometric properties of the scale, construct validity, criterion-related validity, internal consistency coefficient, and test-retest reliability were addressed. According to the findings, item 10 in the original form was removed from the scale due to its factor loading being below .30. The results of Exploratory Factor Analysis indicated that the scale demonstrated a single-factor structure, and this factor consisted of two subcomponents. Confirmatory Factor Analysis also confirmed the factor structure of the scale. In addition, a moderate positive correlation was found between adolescents’ self-compassion scores and subjective well-being scores, while a moderate negative correlation was found between self-compassion scores and fear of self-compassion scores. The internal consistency coefficient of the scale was calculated as .75. Finally, a high level of correlation was observed between the test-retest measurements administered with a 17-day interval. In conclusion, the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form, consisting of 11 items and a single dimension, can be considered a valid and reliable instrument for measuring the self-compassion levels of Turkish adolescents. Keywords: Self-Compassion Scale Short Form, Turkish adaptation, middle school students, high school students

1. INTRODUCTION  
The word self-compassion has been translated into Turkish from the Latin-rooted word “Compassion.” Compassion derives from the combination of the words com (together) + pati (to suffer) (Strauss et al., 2016), and is defined as the ability to respond to the suffering of others in a sensitive, patient, compassionate, and empathetic manner, as well as to recognize that such suffering is an experience that anyone can have (Condon and Feldman Barrett, 2013). Self-compassion, on the other hand, refers to directing one's compassionate attitudes and behaviors toward oneself. Neff (2003a) defines self-compassion as being warm and kind to oneself during difficult times when experiencing pain, distress, failure, and inadequacy, recognizing and accepting one's negative emotions, and understanding that all kinds of challenging experiences are a part of being human. Self-compassion is one of the fundamental concepts of Buddhist teaching, which seeks ways to live wisely and is based on love, compassion, empathy, and composure/equanimity in doing so (Wallace and Shapiro, 2006). According to Buddhist philosophy, suffering, failures, and difficult experiences are part of human life; almost everyone, by virtue of being human, endures painful experiences, and this is inevitable (Rubin, 2013). The important thing is to be able to cope appropriately with painful and challenging experiences. Living wisely is only possible by coping effectively with suffering and challenging situations (Thurman, 2006). Self-compassion is also considered one of the healthy ways to cope with suffering and difficult experiences (Neff, 2003a). Self-compassion is a construct consisting of three components, each with both a positive and negative dimension. The first of these is self-kindness versus self-judgment. Self-kindness versus self-judgment is concerned with the response one gives to emotional suffering and challenging situations (Neff et al., in press). This subdimension describes the attitude a person has toward themselves in the face of suffering and difficulties as a position between self-kindness and self-judgment. Self-kindness means adopting an attitude toward oneself that is gentle, kind, and understanding in the face of suffering, failures, and inadequacies, as well as being able to provide oneself with the necessary care and attention (Neff, 2003b). Conversely, self-judgment can be seen as taking a critical, punitive, and self-deprecating attitude toward oneself in response to suffering, failures, and inadequacies. The second component is common humanity versus isolation. This sub-factor relates to the awareness that painful and challenging experiences are part of being human. It refers to cognitive processing about a painful or challenging experience (Neff et al., in press). Being aware of common humanity means recognizing that difficult and painful experiences are, in fact, experienced by many other people as well, and that experiencing pain is a natural part of being human. A person who is aware of common humanity takes the attitude, “The challenging experience I am going through relates to my humanity; this could happen to most people, and nearly everyone can encounter difficult experiences in their life” (Neff, 2003a). On the other hand, isolation is when a person sees their challenges, suffering, failures, and inadequacies as experiences unique only to themselves. The final subcomponent is mindfulness versus over-identification. Mindfulness versus over-identification involves seeing and understanding one's suffering and failures, and witnessing the resulting negative emotions without judgment (Neff et al., in press). Mindfulness means allowing emotions and experiences to be present without labeling them as good-bad or beautiful-ugly, staying present in the moment, directing one's attention to the present, and maintaining balance in thoughts and emotions (Brown and Ryan, 2003; Neff, 2003a). In contrast, over-identification refers to defining oneself by one’s emotions (e.g., “I am a hopeless person”), excessively identifying with situations, and believing that difficult and painful experiences will persist forever rather than pass. As a result, self-compassion has been defined as a construct composed of three factors, each comprising a positive (self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness) and a negative (self-judgment, isolation, and over-identification) structure (Costa et al., 2016). Thus, self-compassion can be considered as a whole consisting of six subdimensions (Neff, 2003b); these six subdimensions can also be examined under two themes, positive and negative (Bengtsson, Söderström, and Terjestam, 2016; Costa et al., 2016). This is because the subdimensions of self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness reflect a positive, self-compassionate attitude, while self-judgment, isolation, and over-identification reflect a negative, self-critical attitude (Costa et al., 2016). Studies conducted abroad have reported a positive relationship between self-compassion and life satisfaction (Bluth and Blanton, 2012), happiness, optimism (Neff, Rude, and Kirkpatrick, 2007), need satisfaction, self-esteem, self-acceptance (Neff, 2003b), and psychological resilience (Neff and McGehee, 2009). Similarly, studies conducted in our country have shown that self-compassion is positively associated with concepts that predict positive mental health, such as life satisfaction (Tel and Sarı, 2016), self-enhancing humor and communication skills (Akyol, 2011), social support (Akkaya, 2011), mindfulness and resilience (Aydın Sünbül, 2016), as well as positive perceptions of mother, father, and self (Andiç, 2013). On the other hand, studies conducted in our country have found a negative relationship between self-compassion and depression, anxiety, worry, anger, stress (Andıç, 2013; Temel, 2015), problematic internet use (Yiğit, 2015), difficulties in emotion regulation (Aydın Sünbül, 2016), loneliness (Akın, 2010b), and cognitive distortions related to relationships (Akın, 2010a). Similarly, studies conducted abroad have also found that self-compassion is negatively associated with depression (Reas, 2010), anxiety (Pauley and McPherson, 2010), post-traumatic stress disorder (Thompson and Waltz, 2008), and eating disorders (Ferreira, Pinto-Gouveia, Duarte, 2013). Based on this, it can be said that self-compassion is a variable that determines positive mental health (Neff, 2003a). This concept, introduced to the psychology literature by Neff (2003a), was measured only by the “Self-Compassion Scale” until 2011. In the literature of our country, the “Self-Compassion Scale” has appeared as the Self-Understanding Scale (Deniz, Kesici, and Sümer, 2008) and the Self-Sensitivity Scale (Akın, Akın, and Abacı, 2007). The Self-Compassion Scale Short Form was developed by Raes, Pommier, Neff, and Van Gucht (2011) as a more practical alternative to the long form in terms of time. It is recommended that this short form of the scale be used especially in studies where the total score will be used (Raes, Pommier, Neff, and Van Gucht, 2011). The Self-Compassion Scale Short Form consists of items taken from the 26-item Self-Compassion Scale (Neff, 2003b). In order to create the short form, two items for each subcomponent of self-compassion were included in the scale. The positive subcomponents are Self-Kindness, Common Humanity, and Mindfulness, while the negative ones are Self-Judgment, Isolation, and Over-Identification. Thus, the 12-item Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF), consisting of both positive and negative components, was developed. It is observed that this scale has recently started to be used in Western literature, particularly due to its ease of use (Neff et al., in press). The aim of this study by Musa Yıldırım and Tuğba Sarı is to adapt the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form into Turkish and to examine its psychometric properties among adolescents. It is considered that introducing the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form to Turkish will offer convenience in terms of time during the implementation phase of research conducted with adolescents. 2.1. Research Model

Procedure
To conduct the validity and reliability study of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF), Kristin Neff was first contacted via email and the necessary permissions were obtained. Subsequently, the English version of the scale was sent to five faculty members working in the field of guidance and psychological counseling, and they were asked to translate the scale items. The translated items received from the five faculty members were reviewed by the researchers, resulting in the formation of the Turkish version of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form. Before the created Turkish form was administered to the sample group, it was reviewed by the researchers with two groups of 10 students each, comprised of middle school and high school students, to assess whether the scale items were understood. It was found that the scale items were sufficiently understood by both middle and high school students, and the scale was subsequently administered to the sample group. The data obtained were analyzed using the SPSS 22.0 and Lisrel 8.72 software packages. 2.4. Measurement Tools
In this section, the Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale and the Fear of Compassion Scale, which were used to examine the criterion-related validity of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form, are introduced. 2.4.1. Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale  
The Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale is a measurement tool developed by Eryılmaz (2009) for use in happiness research conducted with adolescents. The scale is a Likert-type instrument consisting of 15 items and 4 factors. Due to their structure, these factors are named “Satisfaction in Family Relationships,” “Satisfaction in Relationships with Significant Others,” “Life Satisfaction,” and “Positive Emotions.” Each item on the scale is scored from 1 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Higher scores obtained from the scale indicate a greater presence of the measured characteristic. This tool can be assessed based on the properties of its subscales or using the total score. There are no items on the scale that should be reverse scored. As a result of the reliability analysis, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was calculated as 0.83 for the Family Relationships subfactor, 0.73 for the Satisfaction in Relationships with Significant Others subfactor, 0.81 for the Life Satisfaction subfactor, and 0.66 for the Positive Emotions subfactor. In the current study, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as .894. 2.4.2. Fear of Compassion Scale  
The Fear of Compassion Scale was developed by Gilbert, McEwan, Matos, and Rivis (2011) and adapted into Turkish by Necef and Deniz (2018). The scale measures fear of compassion in three subdimensions: “Fear of Expressing Compassion and Understanding to Others,” “Fear of Responding to Compassion from Others,” and “Fear of Expressing Compassion and Understanding to Oneself.” The scale is a Likert-type measurement tool consisting of a total of 35 items. Each subscale is scored separately. In this study, only the items in the subdimension “Fear of Expressing Compassion and Understanding to Oneself” were used. The construct validity of the scale was examined via Confirmatory Factor Analysis, and three items were removed from the scale because their factor loadings were below 0.30. Therefore, while the original scale contains 38 items, the Turkish version consists of 35 items. As a result, the fit indices of the CFA are as follows: χ2 (552, N = 654) = 1631.68, χ2/df = 2.96, CFI = .90, IFI = .90, SRMR = .058, RMSEA = .055, 90% CI. (.052 – .058). The Cronbach’s alpha value was examined for the internal consistency coefficient of the scale, and accordingly, an alpha value of 0.83 was calculated for the Fear of Responding to Compassion from Others subscale, 0.93 for the Fear of Showing Understanding and Compassion to Oneself subscale, 0.83 for the Fear of Showing Understanding and Compassion to Others subscale, and 0.92 for the entire Fear of Compassion Scale. For the criterion-related validity of the scale, the relationship between the scores obtained from the Fear of Compassion Scale and the scores obtained from the Self-Compassion Scale and the Life Satisfaction Scale was examined, and it was found that there was a significant relationship between these measures. In the present study, the internal consistency coefficient of the Fear of Showing Understanding and Compassion to Oneself subscale was calculated as 0.91. In addition, to test the validity of the scale in an adolescent sample, the factor structure of the scale was examined using Confirmatory Factor Analysis. The analysis showed that the chi-square value was statistically significant (χ2=494.49, N=800, p=0.00). When the fit indices of the CFA analysis were examined, the RMSEA was 0.075, RMSR was 0.070, GFI was 0.92, NFI was 0.97, CFI was 0.97, and NNFI was 0.97. Accordingly, it can be said that the RMSEA, RMSR, and GFI values are at an acceptable level, while the NFI, CFI, and NNFI values indicate an excellent fit. It was observed that the single factor found in both the original version of the Fear of Compassion Scale’s Fear of Showing Compassion to Oneself subscale (Gilbert, McEwan, Matos, and Rivis, 2011) and in the adaptation studies in Turkey (Necef and Deniz, 2018) was confirmed, and the factor loadings of the scale items ranged between 0.43 and 0.76. Thus, the Fear of Showing Compassion to Oneself subscale of the Fear of Compassion Scale can be considered a valid and reliable measurement tool for use with adolescents. 3. FINDINGS
3.1. Findings Regarding Exploratory Factor Analysis  
Factor analysis is a multivariate statistical method that aims to discover and identify a small number of conceptually meaningful and uncorrelated new variables by grouping together p related variables (Büyüköztürk, 2004). In Exploratory Factor Analysis, procedures are carried out with the aim of identifying factors based on the relationships among variables. In the present study, EFA was utilized to examine the factor structure of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF). Before conducting EFA, the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) coefficient and Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity were used to assess the suitability of the dataset for factor analysis. Accordingly, it was found that the dataset had a KMO coefficient of .81 and a Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity χ2 value of 937.456 (p<0.05). Since the KMO coefficient was greater than .50 and the Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity was statistically significant, the dataset was considered suitable for EFA (Çokluk, Şekercioğlu, and Büyüköztürk, 2012). Thus, EFA was conducted, and due to the existence of relationships among the identified factors in the analysis, the oblimin (direct oblimin) method, which is among the oblique rotation methods, was employed (Tabachnick and Fidell, 2015). In the analysis, it was observed that the factor loading of Item 10 was below 0.30. As is known, the factor loading value is a coefficient that explains the relationship of the items with the factors, and it is expected to be greater than 0.30 (Büyüköztürk, 2004: 118; Floyd and Widaman, 1995). Based on this, Item 10 was excluded from the scale due to its low factor loading value, and the EFA was rerun. The findings obtained from this second analysis are presented in Table 2. Findings Regarding the Confirmatory Factor Analysis

Confirmatory Factor Analysis is a method used to verify the extent to which data collected with a measurement tool fit the theoretical structure underlying the instrument (Aytaç and Ongen, 2012). In the present study, it was aimed to confirm the compatibility of the factor structure of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF) with both theoretical foundations and the findings obtained from the Exploratory Factor Analysis. In this context, CFA was conducted on a data set of 339 individuals. The analysis showed that the chi-square value was statistically significant (χ2=90.05, N=339, p=0.00). When the fit indices of the CFA were examined, RMSEA=0.06, RMSR=0.095, GFI=0.96, NFI=0.91, CFI=0.95, and NNFI=0.94 were calculated. According to these values, the RMSR, GFI, NFI, and NNFI values for the data set indicated an excellent fit (Bentler and Bonett, 1980; Schermelleh-Engel and Moosbrugger, 2003; Marsh, Hau, Artelt, Baumert, and Peschar, 2006), while the RMSEA value was found to be at an acceptable level of fit (Byrne and Campbell, 1999). To examine the internal consistency level of the scale, the Cronbach’s alpha value was assessed. As a result of the statistical analysis, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the first subfactor of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form was calculated as 0.73, while the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the second subfactor was calculated as 0.71. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as 0.75. 3.5. Findings Regarding Test-Retest Reliability
In order to calculate the test-retest reliability of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF), data were collected twice from a sample group with a 17-day interval, and the relationship between these two measurements was examined. 4. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION  
In this study, which examined the psychometric properties of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF) among Turkish adolescents, the structural validity, criterion-related validity, internal consistency coefficient, and test-retest reliability coefficient of the scale were analyzed. As a result of the Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) conducted to examine structural validity, it was observed that the factor loading of Item 10 was below 0.30, and thus this item was removed from the scale. According to the EFA, it was also determined that the SCS-SF has a general factor, and this general factor consists of two subcomponents (Büyüköztürk, 2004: 127). The negative items explain 29.88% of the total variance, while the second factor explains 14.99% of the total variance. Thus, together, the two factors explain 44.87% of the total variance. In the subsequent Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), it was found that the original SCS-SF is represented by a model consistent with its theoretical foundation (Bengtsson, Söderström, and Terjestam, 2016; Costa et al., 2016; Neff et al., in press), in which the positive items load on one subdimension and the negative items on another. The results of the factor analyses confirmed that the SCS-SF has a structure consisting of a single factor made up of two complementary components (positive component and negative component). When examining the criterion-related validity of the scale, a negative and moderate relationship was found between the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form and the Fear of Compassion Scale’s “fear of showing compassion to oneself” subdimension, and a positive and moderate relationship was found with the Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale. Studies exploring the relationship between self-compassion and fear of compassion (Necef and Deniz, 2018) and subjective well-being (Zessin, Dickhäuser, and Garbade, 2015) show that the current findings are consistent with previously reported results. Additionally, data were collected from the same group 17 days apart with the SCS-SF, and a high level of correlation was found between the two measurements. This indicates that the SCS-SF measures a stable construct. With these results, the SCS-SF has become an 11-item, five-point Likert-type, self-report scale. Due to its brevity, ease of application and evaluation, it is considered that the scale will meet an important need in studies aimed at measuring self-compassion among adolescents in Turkish society. In conclusion, (1) the SCS-SF is a valid and reliable measurement tool for assessing self-compassion among middle and high school students in the Turkish cultural context, (2) the SCS-SF exhibits meaningful correlations with subjective well-being and fear of showing compassion to oneself, and (3) the SCS-SF has a unidimensional structure. It is recommended to use the total score of the SCS-SF in studies aiming to measure self-compassion. Turkish Adaptation of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form: Validity…

TURKISH ADAPTATION OF THE SELF-COMPASSION SCALE SHORT FORM: VALIDITY AND RELIABILITY STUDY*
Musa YILDIRIM**
Tuğba SARI*** ABSTRACT The aim of this study was to examine the psychometric properties of the Turkish version of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form among adolescents. For this purpose, data were collected from 800 adolescents—400 middle school students and 400 high school students. In order to examine the psychometric properties of the scale, construct validity, criterion-related validity, internal consistency coefficient, and test-retest reliability were addressed. According to the findings, item 10 in the original form was removed from the scale due to its factor loading being below .30. The results of Exploratory Factor Analysis indicated that the scale demonstrated a single-factor structure, and this factor consisted of two subcomponents. Confirmatory Factor Analysis also confirmed the factor structure of the scale. In addition, a moderate positive correlation was found between adolescents’ self-compassion scores and subjective well-being scores, while a moderate negative correlation was found between self-compassion scores and fear of self-compassion scores. The internal consistency coefficient of the scale was calculated as .75. Finally, a high level of correlation was observed between the test-retest measurements administered with a 17-day interval.

discourses.source_txt: Compassion derives from the combination of the words com (together) + pati (to suffer) (Strauss et al., 2016), and is defined as the ability to respond to the suffering of others in a sensitive, patient, compassionate, and empathetic manner, as well as to recognize that such suffering is an experience that anyone can have (Condon and Feldman Barrett, 2013). Self-compassion, on the other hand, refers to directing one's compassionate attitudes and behaviors toward oneself.
discourses.translated_txt: Şefkat, com (birlikte) + pati (cıkmak) kelimelerinin birleşiminden kaynaklanır (Strauss et al., 2016), ve başkalarının acılarına hassas, sabırlı, şefkatli ve empatici bir şekilde cevap verme yeteneği olarak tanımlanır.

discourses.source_txt: Neff (2003a) defines self-compassion as being warm and kind to oneself during difficult times when experiencing pain, distress, failure, and inadequacy, recognizing and accepting one's negative emotions, and understanding that all kinds of challenging experiences are a part of being human.
discourses.translated_txt: Neff (2003a) kendi kendine merhamet, acı, sıkıntı, başarısızlık ve yetersizlik yaşadığınız zor zamanlarda kendine sıcak ve nazik olmak, kişinin olumsuz duygularını tanımak ve kabul etmek ve her türlü zorlu deneyimlerin insan olmanın bir parçası olduğunu anlamak olarak tanımlar.

discourses.source_txt: Self-compassion is one of the fundamental concepts of Buddhist teaching, which seeks ways to live wisely and is based on love, compassion, empathy, and composure/equanimity in doing so (Wallace and Shapiro, 2006).
discourses.translated_txt: Öz-öğrür, bilge yaşama yollarını arayan ve bunu yaparken sevgi, şefkat, empati ve sakinlik / eşitlik üzerine kurulan Budist öğretisinin temel kavramlarından biridir (Wallace ve Shapiro, 2006).

discourses.source_txt: According to Buddhist philosophy, suffering, failures, and difficult experiences are part of human life; almost everyone, by virtue of being human, endures painful experiences, and this is inevitable (Rubin, 2013). The important thing is to be able to cope appropriately with painful and challenging experiences. Living wisely is only possible by coping effectively with suffering and challenging situations (Thurman, 2006). Self-compassion is also considered one of the healthy ways to cope with suffering and difficult experiences (Neff, 2003a). Self-compassion is a construct consisting of three components, each with both a positive and negative dimension. The first of these is self-kindness versus self-judgment. Self-kindness versus self-judgment is concerned with the response one gives to emotional suffering and challenging situations (Neff et al., in press). This subdimension describes the attitude a person has toward themselves in the face of suffering and difficulties as a position between self-kindness and self-judgment. Self-kindness means adopting an attitude toward oneself that is gentle, kind, and understanding in the face of suffering, failures, and inadequacies, as well as being able to provide oneself with the necessary care and attention (Neff, 2003b). Conversely, self-judgment can be seen as taking a critical, punitive, and self-deprecating attitude toward oneself in response to suffering, failures, and inadequacies. The second component is common humanity versus isolation. This sub-factor relates to the awareness that painful and challenging experiences are part of being human. It refers to cognitive processing about a painful or challenging experience (Neff et al., in press). Being aware of common humanity means recognizing that difficult and painful experiences are, in fact, experienced by many other people as well, and that experiencing pain is a natural part of being human. A person who is aware of common humanity takes the attitude, “The challenging experience I am going through relates to my humanity; this could happen to most people, and nearly everyone can encounter difficult experiences in their life” (Neff, 2003a). On the other hand, isolation is when a person sees their challenges, suffering, failures, and inadequacies as experiences unique only to themselves. The final subcomponent is mindfulness versus over-identification. Mindfulness versus over-identification involves seeing and understanding one's suffering and failures, and witnessing the resulting negative emotions without judgment (Neff et al., in press). Mindfulness means allowing emotions and experiences to be present without labeling them as good-bad or beautiful-ugly, staying present in the moment, directing one's attention to the present, and maintaining balance in thoughts and emotions (Brown and Ryan, 2003; Neff, 2003a). In contrast, over-identification refers to defining oneself by one’s emotions (e.g., “I am a hopeless person”), excessively identifying with situations, and believing that difficult and painful experiences will persist forever rather than pass. As a result, self-compassion has been defined as a construct composed of three factors, each comprising a positive (self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness) and a negative (self-judgment, isolation, and over-identification) structure (Costa et al., 2016). Thus, self-compassion can be considered as a whole consisting of six subdimensions (Neff, 2003b); these six subdimensions can also be examined under two themes, positive and negative (Bengtsson, Söderström, and Terjestam, 2016; Costa et al., 2016). This is because the subdimensions of self-kindness, common humanity, and mindfulness reflect a positive, self-compassionate attitude, while self-judgment, isolation, and over-identification reflect a negative, self-critical attitude (Costa et al., 2016).

discourses.source_txt: Studies conducted abroad have reported a positive relationship between self-compassion and life satisfaction (Bluth and Blanton, 2012), happiness, optimism (Neff, Rude, and Kirkpatrick, 2007), need satisfaction, self-esteem, self-acceptance (Neff, 2003b), and psychological resilience (Neff and McGehee, 2009).

discourses.source_txt: Similarly, studies conducted in our country have shown that self-compassion is positively associated with concepts that predict positive mental health, such as life satisfaction (Tel and Sarı, 2016), self-enhancing humor and communication skills (Akyol, 2011), social support (Akkaya, 2011), mindfulness and resilience (Aydın Sünbül, 2016), as well as positive perceptions of mother, father, and self (Andiç, 2013).

discourses.source_txt: On the other hand, studies conducted in our country have found a negative relationship between self-compassion and depression, anxiety, worry, anger, stress (Andıç, 2013; Temel, 2015), problematic internet use (Yiğit, 2015), difficulties in emotion regulation (Aydın Sünbül, 2016), loneliness (Akın, 2010b), and cognitive distortions related to relationships (Akın, 2010a).

Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale  
The Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale is a measurement tool developed by Eryılmaz (2009) for use in happiness research conducted with adolescents. The scale is a Likert-type instrument consisting of 15 items and 4 factors. Due to their structure, these factors are named “Satisfaction in Family Relationships,” “Satisfaction in Relationships with Significant Others,” “Life Satisfaction,” and “Positive Emotions.” Each item on the scale is scored from 1 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Higher scores obtained from the scale indicate a greater presence of the measured characteristic. This tool can be assessed based on the properties of its subscales or using the total score. There are no items on the scale that should be reverse scored. As a result of the reliability analysis, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient was calculated as 0.83 for the Family Relationships subfactor, 0.73 for the Satisfaction in Relationships with Significant Others subfactor, 0.81 for the Life Satisfaction subfactor, and 0.66 for the Positive Emotions subfactor. In the current study, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as .894.

Findings Regarding Exploratory Factor Analysis  
Factor analysis is a multivariate statistical method that aims to discover and identify a small number of conceptually meaningful and uncorrelated new variables by grouping together p related variables (Büyüköztürk, 2004). In Exploratory Factor Analysis, procedures are carried out with the aim of identifying factors based on the relationships among variables. In the present study, EFA was utilized to examine the factor structure of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF). Before conducting EFA, the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) coefficient and Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity were used to assess the suitability of the dataset for factor analysis. Accordingly, it was found that the dataset had a KMO coefficient of .81 and a Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity χ2 value of 937.456 (p<0.05). Since the KMO coefficient was greater than .50 and the Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity was statistically significant, the dataset was considered suitable for EFA (Çokluk, Şekercioğlu, and Büyüköztürk, 2012). Thus, EFA was conducted, and due to the existence of relationships among the identified factors in the analysis, the oblimin (direct oblimin) method, which is among the oblique rotation methods, was employed (Tabachnick and Fidell, 2015). In the analysis, it was observed that the factor loading of Item 10 was below 0.30. As is known, the factor loading value is a coefficient that explains the relationship of the items with the factors, and it is expected to be greater than 0.30 (Büyüköztürk, 2004: 118; Floyd and Widaman, 1995). Based on this, Item 10 was excluded from the scale due to its low factor loading value, and the EFA was rerun. The findings obtained from this second analysis are presented in Table 2.

Findings Regarding the Confirmatory Factor Analysis

Confirmatory Factor Analysis is a method used to verify the extent to which data collected with a measurement tool fit the theoretical structure underlying the instrument (Aytaç and Ongen, 2012). In the present study, it was aimed to confirm the compatibility of the factor structure of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF) with both theoretical foundations and the findings obtained from the Exploratory Factor Analysis. In this context, CFA was conducted on a data set of 339 individuals. The analysis showed that the chi-square value was statistically significant (χ2=90.05, N=339, p=0.00). When the fit indices of the CFA were examined, RMSEA=0.06, RMSR=0.095, GFI=0.96, NFI=0.91, CFI=0.95, and NNFI=0.94 were calculated. According to these values, the RMSR, GFI, NFI, and NNFI values for the data set indicated an excellent fit (Bentler and Bonett, 1980; Schermelleh-Engel and Moosbrugger, 2003; Marsh, Hau, Artelt, Baumert, and Peschar, 2006), while the RMSEA value was found to be at an acceptable level of fit (Byrne and Campbell, 1999). The factor loadings for the two-dimensional model obtained from the CFA are shown in Figure 1.

Findings Related to Internal Consistency

To examine the internal consistency level of the scale, the Cronbach’s alpha value was assessed. As a result of the statistical analysis, the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the first subfactor of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form was calculated as 0.73, while the Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the second subfactor was calculated as 0.71. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as 0.75.

Findings Regarding Test-Retest Reliability
In order to calculate the test-retest reliability of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF), data were collected twice from a sample group with a 17-day interval, and the relationship between these two measurements was examined. Statistical analysis revealed a high level of correlation between the two measurements (r= .840, p<0.01).

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION  
In this study, which examined the psychometric properties of the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form (SCS-SF) among Turkish adolescents, the structural validity, criterion-related validity, internal consistency coefficient, and test-retest reliability coefficient of the scale were analyzed. As a result of the Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) conducted to examine structural validity, it was observed that the factor loading of Item 10 was below 0.30, and thus this item was removed from the scale. According to the EFA, it was also determined that the SCS-SF has a general factor, and this general factor consists of two subcomponents (Büyüköztürk, 2004: 127). The negative items explain 29.88% of the total variance, while the second factor explains 14.99% of the total variance. Thus, together, the two factors explain 44.87% of the total variance. In the subsequent Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), it was found that the original SCS-SF is represented by a model consistent with its theoretical foundation (Bengtsson, Söderström, and Terjestam, 2016; Costa et al., 2016; Neff et al., in press), in which the positive items load on one subdimension and the negative items on another. The results of the factor analyses confirmed that the SCS-SF has a structure consisting of a single factor made up of two complementary components (positive component and negative component). When examining the criterion-related validity of the scale, a negative and moderate relationship was found between the Self-Compassion Scale Short Form and the Fear of Compassion Scale’s “fear of showing compassion to oneself” subdimension, and a positive and moderate relationship was found with the Adolescent Subjective Well-Being Scale. Studies exploring the relationship between self-compassion and fear of compassion (Necef and Deniz, 2018) and subjective well-being (Zessin, Dickhäuser, and Garbade, 2015) show that the current findings are consistent with previously reported results. Additionally, data were collected from the same group 17 days apart with the SCS-SF, and a high level of correlation was found between the two measurements. This indicates that the SCS-SF measures a stable construct. With these results, the SCS-SF has become an 11-item, five-point Likert-type, self-report scale. Due to its brevity, ease of application and evaluation, it is considered that the scale will meet an important need in studies aimed at measuring self-compassion among adolescents in Turkish society. In conclusion, (1) the SCS-SF is a valid and reliable measurement tool for assessing self-compassion among middle and high school students in the Turkish cultural context, (2) the SCS-SF exhibits meaningful correlations with subjective well-being and fear of showing compassion to oneself, and (3) the SCS-SF has a unidimensional structure. It is recommended to use the total score of the SCS-SF in studies aiming to measure self-compassion.
